title: Youth has gone
hookLine: youth passes and old age conquers the body (Salok M9, ang 1428)

lines: A STRANGER IN THE SHOP WINDOW.
THE MIRROR KEEPS ITS OWN COUNT.
cards: A shop window catches your reflection, unexpectedly, and for half a second the person in it is a stranger. Then the face comes into focus. When did that happen?
The gray at the temples, the line between the eyebrows, the oof that now comes with sitting down. The calendar keeps one count; the mirror keeps another. A whole industry promises to stop the clock.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks don't sell anything. They tell the truth about the clock, and then ask a better question.

teach.h: TARNAAPO: YOUTH, GONE JUST LIKE THAT.
teach.b: One of the early saloks begins tarnaapo io hee gaio, leeo jaraa tan jeet. In paraphrase: youth has passed away just like that, and old age has conquered the body. Tarnaapo is youth, the years of strength.
Io hee, just like that, without anyone noticing.
And jaraa is old age, pictured as a conqueror that has taken the body's territory. It's an honest line, with no softening.
But listen to its second line, which you met on day five hundred ninety: says Nanak, O mind, turn to the Lord, the time is slipping by. Old age in these couplets isn't the enemy to defeat.
It's a teacher pointing at the clock.
The question isn't how to stay young. It's what you're doing with the age you are. Sikh life has room for every stage.
Children learn to sit in the sangat and sing. Young people work, marry, raise families, and serve. Elders are honored for what they've carried.

teach.h: EACH AGE REMEMBERS IN ITS WAY.
teach.b: Each age can remember the Lord in its own way: a child's simple Waheguru, a parent's tired prayer at the end of a long day, an elder's slow, steady simran. None is second best.
The salok tells us youth goes. It doesn't say anything is lost that can't be offered at the next age. The body changes its count.
The soul's work, remembering, is the same at seven, at thirty-seven, at seventy-seven.

how: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks on youth and old age at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; in the gurdwara, children, adults and elders sit and sing together.

o: a mirror that shows the years
old age, the conqueror of the body

games.q: youth has gone — tap the pairs.

s: the salok promises a way to stay young
it tells the truth: youth passes and old age conquers the body.
the salok pictures old age as a conqueror taking the body
leeo jaraa tan jeet: old age has won the body.
in Sikh life, remembering the Lord belongs only to the old
every age remembers in its own way, from a child's Waheguru to an elder's simran.

games.q: you catch your reflection and see the years. what does the salok turn your attention to?
o: what you're doing with the age you are.
games.why: the salok admits youth has gone and calls the mind to the Lord. the question isn't how to stay young, but how to use this age.

practice: Scan slowly from feet to head, and wherever you notice something that's changed with the years, a stiff knee, tired eyes, a sore back, pause there and thank it instead of resenting it.
Thank the feet for every mile, the hands for everything they've carried, the heart for beating through every year so far. If you pray, you can thank Waheguru for this body, at exactly this age.

wordCard.voice: Tarnaapo, youth, the years of strength. The salok says it passes just like that, and jaraa, old age, conquers the body; and every age can still turn to the Lord.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jaraa, old age. The salok says jaraa has conquered the body.

carryVoice: Your line: every age is his. A gray hair can be a reminder, not a verdict. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, 'tarnaapo io hee gaio leeo jaraa tan jeet' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1426)
